title: Fewest Straight Cuts for Equal Slices
statement:
You want to split a round cake into n equal slices. You may make two kinds of straight cuts:

  • a full cut: a line through the centre from one edge to the opposite edge;
  • a half cut: a segment from the centre to one point on the edge.

Return the smallest number of cuts that splits the cake into exactly n equal slices. With n = 1 the whole cake is the slice.

examples.why: Three full cuts 60° apart give 6 equal slices. Each full cut makes two edges at once.
Five slice edges sit 72° apart. No two of them are opposite each other, so no full cut can be used and every edge needs its own half cut.

hints: Equal slices need n edges from the centre, spaced 360/n degrees apart. How many edges does each kind of cut produce?
A full cut produces two edges, but only if both are opposite each other, 180° apart. When does an edge have a partner exactly opposite?
For even n every edge has an opposite partner, so n/2 full cuts. For odd n none does, so n half cuts. And n = 1 needs nothing.

explain.intuition:
Think about the edges of the slices, the radii from the centre. For n equal slices you need n radii spaced 360/n degrees apart. A half cut draws one radius; a full cut draws two radii, but only two that are exactly opposite.

If n is even, every radius has its opposite partner among the others (half the circle is a whole number of slices), so you can pair them all: n/2 cuts. If n is odd, 180° is not a multiple of 360/n, so no pair is opposite and every radius costs a cut: n. The single exception is n = 1: one slice is the whole cake and needs no edge at all, while a single half cut would leave the cake in one piece but not split.
pitfalls: Returning n / 2 rounded up for odd n. Full cuts cannot be used at all when n is odd.
Returning 1 for n = 1. The whole cake already is the single slice.
Returning n for n = 2: one full cut makes both edges.

solutions.title: Parity case split
solutions.idea: Pair opposite radii into full cuts when n is even; otherwise every radius is a half cut. n = 1 needs no cut.

followups: Cuts may now be any straight line, not only through the centre, and slices need equal area but not equal shape. Does the answer change?
How many slices, at most, can k straight cuts in any position produce?
